title: Three Million Prescriptions in Five Months. The Obesity Pill Is Here.
excerpt: Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill is now one of the fastest pharmaceutical launches in US history. With 80 per cent of users new to GLP-1 therapy, the oral obesity revolution is pulling in people who would never have taken a weekly injection — including the South Asians who need it most.
body:
One prescription filled every five seconds. Three million in just over five months. Wegovy in pill form is now one of the strongest pharmaceutical launches in United States history by volume, and the number that should alarm public health officials is not the sales figure — it is who is showing up.

More than 80 per cent of Wegovy pill prescriptions have gone to people who were never on GLP-1 therapy before. They were not switching from injections. They were not on Ozempic for diabetes. They were, until January 2026, simply untreated — living with obesity, often with related cardiovascular risk, and doing nothing about it pharmacologically.

The pill changed the equation. And for South Asians, who carry the highest population-level risk for the metabolic conditions these drugs target, the shift may matter more than for any other demographic group.

The Injection Barrier Was Real

Semaglutide, the active ingredient in Wegovy, has been available as a weekly injection since 2021. The clinical data was never in doubt — 15 to 17 per cent body weight reduction in trials, with cardiovascular benefits that earned it an FDA label for reducing the risk of heart attack, stroke, and death in adults with obesity and heart disease.

But injection-based therapies carry a psychological and cultural overhead that clinical data cannot fully capture. For South Asian patients, the barrier is compounded. Research consistently shows that South Asians underutilise preventive medication, partly due to stigma around chronic disease treatment and partly due to cultural preference for dietary and lifestyle interventions. An injection that must be self-administered weekly, refrigerated, and explained to family members adds friction at every step.

A daily pill, taken with water, resolves most of that. Novo Nordisk's data suggests the market agrees: Wegovy pill is not cannibalising existing injection prescriptions. It is creating entirely new patients.

The South Asian Risk Profile

The World Health Organisation lowered the BMI threshold for obesity classification in Asian populations years ago, recognising that South Asians develop metabolic complications — insulin resistance, visceral fat accumulation, cardiovascular disease — at body mass indices that would be classified as merely "overweight" under Western standards. A South Asian with a BMI of 23 carries metabolic risk equivalent to a European at 25 to 27.

This is not a marginal difference. It means millions of diaspora South Asians who do not consider themselves obese by the numbers on their bathroom scale are, metabolically, candidates for intervention. The arrival of an oral GLP-1 that demonstrably pulls new patients into treatment is relevant precisely because the untreated population is so large.

The Competition Is Getting Fierce

Wegovy is not alone. In April 2026, the FDA approved Eli Lilly's orforglipron — the first non-peptide oral GLP-1 receptor agonist, a daily pill that delivered 12.4 per cent weight loss in trials with no food or water restrictions. Unlike semaglutide, which is a modified peptide and requires careful formulation to survive stomach acid, orforglipron is a small molecule that can be manufactured more cheaply and scaled more easily.

At ADA 2026 in New Orleans, the pipeline deepened further. Novo Nordisk presented Phase 3 results for CagriSema, a combination of semaglutide and a novel amylin analog called cagrilintide, showing significant reductions in both HbA1c and body weight across multiple trials in adults with type 2 diabetes. Innovent Biologics showcased preclinical data for IBI3042, potentially the world's first once-weekly oral small-molecule GLP-1 that outperformed orforglipron in early comparisons.

The direction is clear: oral, convenient, and increasingly effective. The injection era is not over, but its monopoly on potency is ending.

What NRIs Should Know Now

For diaspora South Asians considering treatment, the landscape has shifted in three practical ways.

First, access is wider. Wegovy pill is available at more than 70,000 US pharmacies and through telehealth providers. Commercially insured patients can access it for as low as 25 dollars per month. Starting July 1, 2026, Medicare beneficiaries with obesity will be eligible through Novo Nordisk's new GLP-1 Bridge program at 50 dollars per month.

Second, the clinical evidence now covers cardiovascular protection explicitly. Wegovy is FDA-approved not just for weight loss but for reducing the risk of major cardiovascular events — death, heart attack, stroke — in adults with obesity and known heart disease. For a community where heart disease is the leading killer and often strikes a decade earlier than in European populations, this is not a cosmetic consideration.

Third, the stigma calculus has shifted. Three million prescriptions in five months means GLP-1 therapy is no longer niche. It is becoming a normal part of chronic disease management, as routine as a statin or a blood pressure pill. For South Asian families where medical conversations are often conducted in whispers, normalisation matters.

The pill will not fix the structural barriers — the lack of culturally competent obesity care, the absence of South Asian-specific dosing guidelines, the gap between what insurance covers and what patients need. But it removes the first and most visceral objection many patients had: the needle. And in a population where the need was always greater than the uptake, that alone may move the numbers that matter.

Sources: Novo Nordisk (ADA 2026 press release); AINvest; Novo Nordisk CagriSema REIMAGINE Phase 3 data
